metadata.title: Computer Organization and Architecture Lab
metadata.format: Hybrid (synchronous Zoom lab plus asynchronous work)
metadata.prerequisite: CSC221 - Programming and Algorithms I. Recommended companion: concurrent enrollment in CSC 210 - Computer Organization and Architecture. CSC 210L is a recommended, not required, lab for CSC 210, and no CSC 210 grade depends on it.
metadata.corequisite: CSC210 - Computer Organization and Architecture (recommended, not required)

meetingSchedule.modality: Hybrid. We meet live on Zoom every Tuesday for a 90-minute hands-on session, and you carry the work forward asynchronously between sessions. Labs marked [Completes in class] are sized to finish inside the session; labs marked [Finish on own] deliberately send you home with a working partial circuit and a short, clearly stated remaining task (typically 45-90 minutes).
meetingSchedule.zoomLinkHtml: Join the Tuesday lab session (same link every week)

description.catalog: Laboratory course accompanying CSC 210. Hands-on construction of digital logic circuits and assembly-language programs, using circuit simulation and a MIPS runtime simulator to build and test the components of a working processor.
description.expanded:
CSC 210L is the room where you build the machine with your hands. Each Tuesday works the material of that same week's CSC 210 lecture content, after you have seen it - you arrive knowing the concept and leave having built it.

The lab carries one continuous construction sequence. Labs 1-14 build a CPU out of primitive gates, one .circ tab at a time, in a single file you keep all term: gates from NAND, adders and decoders, latches and flip-flops, an 8-bit register, an ALU, a RAM matrix, a register file, a control unit, and finally a complete datapath executing your own instruction set. Interleaved with that, you write MIPS assembly in MARS and watch the registers, stack, and data segment move one instruction at a time - so the hardware and the software explain each other in the same 90 minutes.

This lab scaffolds; it does not gate. Every circuit and program CSC 210 grades remains fully completable by a student who never attends lab. Lab reduces friction, gives you an instructor at your elbow when a circuit fails silently, and gets you started in company rather than alone at 11 PM.

purpose.why: Circuits fail quietly and assembly does exactly what you wrote rather than what you meant. Both are far easier to learn with someone in the room. This lab gives you a guided, supported start on the same builds CSC 210 assesses - the 90 minutes where the tricky part gets demonstrated, the whole room builds in lockstep, and the instructor circulates while you debug. Students who use the lab typically arrive at the final CPU project with a working partial machine rather than a blank file.
purpose.beyond: The lab teaches a debugging method, not just circuits: form a hypothesis, test the first stage that could fail, narrow down, and never guess downstream of a broken signal. Lab 13's debugging clinic makes that explicit, and it is the single most transferable skill in the course. You will also leave with a habit that is worth real points - one file, built continuously, audited weekly, so that nothing is invented at the last minute.

slos: Write, execute and debug small programs or segments of larger programs using an assembly language.
Simulate basic computer architecture, organization and design concepts.
_sloNote: CSLOs supplied by the instructor 2026-08-17 as the Course Outline of Record text for CSC 210L, quoted verbatim as required by college syllabus policy. Both CSLOs are assessed continuously through the weekly completion checks rather than by exam: SLO 1 by the MARS/MIPS work in Labs 5-8, 12, 15, and 16; SLO 2 by the Logisim construction sequence in Labs 1-14 and the simulator experiments in Labs 15-16.

aiPolicy.title: AI Policy for This Course
aiPolicy.approach: Restricted - one sanctioned AI tool, the course AI Tutor. Other AI assistants are not permitted on graded work.
aiPolicy.scopeNote: This policy applies to CSC 210L only, and it is deliberately identical to the CSC 210 policy so that students enrolled in both courses have exactly one rule to follow across the lecture and the lab. Every course sets its own AI policy, and this one is narrower than most. What is permitted in another class - including other computer science classes - is not permitted here unless it is the AI Tutor.
aiPolicy.summary: This course has one approved AI tool: the CSC 210 AI Tutor, a web-based tutor introduced in Week 2. It is a frontier language model tuned specifically for this course - it knows our constraints, our tools, and where we are in the progression. Use it as much as you like. General-purpose AI assistants are not permitted on graded work in this course.
permitted: Use the AI Tutor freely, as often as you want, at any hour. It is available from Week 2 onward and there is no limit on how much you use it. Asking it for help is not a sign you are behind - it is how the tool is meant to be used.

Ask it to explain anything. Why NAND is universal, what a gated D latch is actually doing, why your ripple-carry adder is off by one, what the calling convention expects on the stack. Ask it the same question three different ways until it lands.

Ask it to help you debug your own work. Describe what your circuit does versus what you expected, or paste the assembly that is not behaving, and work through it together. Debugging with the tutor is real learning, not a shortcut - and it is exactly what we do together in lab.
Ask it to check your understanding before a lab or a checkpoint. Have it quiz you, or explain your design back to it and let it find the gap.
required: You build the circuits and you write the assembly. The tutor helps you understand and debug; it does not produce your deliverables. Every .circ tab and every line of MIPS you submit must be work you constructed.

Note substantial AI Tutor help when you submit. One line is enough - for example, "worked through the carry chain with the AI Tutor." This is not a penalty and never costs you points; it tells me where the course content needs to be clearer.

Be able to explain your own work. For any completion check, you should be able to walk me through why each part of your build is there. If you cannot explain it, it is not finished - regardless of whether it appears to work.
notPermitted: General-purpose AI assistants on graded work. ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, and similar tools are not permitted for the weekly lab completion checks, or for any CSC 210 deliverable this lab scaffolds - the Logisim checkpoints, MIPS assignments, quizzes, exams, research paper, or final project.
Submitting AI-generated circuits or code as your own. A .circ file or an assembly listing that you did not build is not your work, whatever produced it.
Handing a partner a solution during peer testing. Lab 16 has you run each other's CPUs on purpose. Finding a classmate's bug is the point; generating their fix is not.
Sharing AI Tutor sessions as a substitute for another student's own build. Helping a classmate think is good; handing them a solution is not.
aiPolicy.whyThisLine: This is not a general suspicion of AI - it is specific to what this course does. The AI Tutor knows our constraints and general-purpose assistants do not. Ask ChatGPT how to build a register file and it will confidently hand you Logisim Evolution components, a built-in RAM block, and a multiplexer where this course requires a decoder - all of which are wrong here, and all of which will cost you a checkpoint in CSC 210. The tutor is tuned to Logisim Classic 2.7.1, primitive-gate construction, decoder-based selection, and the single-file build. Beyond that: both CSLOs require that you write, execute, and debug the programs and simulate the design. A circuit you did not build cannot demonstrate that.
aiPolicy.consequences: Work produced by a non-approved AI tool, or any work submitted as your own that you did not produce, falls under the College Academic Honesty Policy (AP 5500.2) and may result in a zero on the assignment, a failing grade in the course, and referral for disciplinary action. If you are behind and tempted, come to student hours or to Lab 17 instead - an extension is always available and costs you far less.
aiPolicy.uncertainty: If you are not sure whether a tool or a use is allowed, ask before you submit. Asking never counts against you. The short version: if it is the AI Tutor, yes; if it is anything else and the work is graded, no.

schedule._design: Seventeen Tuesday lab sessions, 08/18/2026 - 12/08/2026, inside the 17-week term 08/17/2026 - 12/11/2026. Week numbering and week date ranges match course-csc210-info.json so the lecture and lab outlines line up week for week. Lab Week N works the material of Lecture Week N and meets after that week's lecture content has been introduced. Every structured session follows the same 90-minute arc: framing and demo (~15 min), guided build together (~40 min), independent build (~25 min), debrief and close (~10 min). Lab 17 is a deliberate exception - unstructured open studio. Tuesday resolves every holiday conflict: Labor Day (Mon 9/7), the campus holiday (Fri 9/25), and Veterans Day (Wed 11/11) all fall on non-lab days, and no session is lost. Each lab's completion check is due the following Monday at 11:59 PM, which gives the [Finish on own] labs a full week. Standing constraints in every Logisim lab: Logisim Classic 2.7.1 only, build from primitive gates, decoders for control and address selection, and one .circ file for the entire semester.

phases.title: Phase 1: Digital Foundations (Labs 1-4, Weeks 1-4)
phases.description: Toolchain, gates, arithmetic, and memory. By the end of this phase your semester .circ file holds a NAND-built gate library, an adder, a decoder, and the three memory primitives every later lab instances. Primary CSLO: 2.

topics: Lab 1 — Toolchain Setup & Seeing Binary [Completes in class]
Install and verify Logisim Classic 2.7.1 — and see why Evolution is not acceptable, side by side
Install MARS and confirm the Java runtime works
Create the semester LastName_CSC210.circ file, name your first circuit tab, save it — this file is never replaced
Logisim orientation: toolbar, wiring, input and output pins, probes, the poke tool
First circuit: an 8-bit input pin driving a probe, reading the same byte in hex, unsigned decimal, and binary
Partner conversion drill, verified against the circuit rather than an answer key
MARS orientation: open a provided program, run it, find the Registers and Data Segment panes
assignments: Completion check 1 (10 pts): both tools launch at the correct versions, and your semester .circ file exists with a named first tab
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 1 (Binary & Number Representation). The lab that pays for itself — week-one tool problems otherwise eat week-two learning time. Download links for Windows and macOS are on the course SharePoint. Leaves lab with: a working toolchain, the semester file created, and fluency reading a byte three ways.

topics: Lab 2 — Gates from NAND [Completes in class]
Build AND, OR, and NOT using only NAND gates, each in its own tab, verified by exhaustive poking
Build XOR from NAND (5 gates) — the first circuit where you must think rather than copy
De Morgan verification circuit: drive NOT(A AND B) and NOT(A) OR NOT(B) from the same inputs into an XOR that lights an LED if they ever disagree. It never lights — a proof you can poke
Logisim technique: subcircuits, establishing the build-once-reuse-forever pattern the whole course depends on
Splitters and tunnels for wire management, introduced before circuits get wide
assignments: Completion check 2 (10 pts): NAND-built AND, OR, NOT, and XOR tabs plus the self-checking De Morgan circuit, all in the semester file
Meet the AI Tutor — the one approved AI tool for this course and CSC 210, available from this week onward
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 2 (Logic Gates). The AI Tutor comes online this week — see the AI Policy under Policies & Resources. College deadline: 8/28/2026 is the last day to add, to drop without a notation, and for an enrollment-fee refund.

topics: Lab 3 — Adders and Decoders [Finish on own]
Together: half adder from gates, then a full adder from two half adders plus OR, verified across all 8 input combinations
Together: chain four full adders into a 4-bit ripple-carry adder and watch the carry propagate on probes
Together: build a 2-to-4 decoder from gates
Decoder vs. multiplexer — a decoder answers "which one do I activate?", a mux answers "which one do I let through?". Build a 2-to-1 mux too, so the distinction is concrete rather than asserted
On your own: extend the ripple-carry adder to 8 bits and build the 3-to-8 decoder
assignments: Completion check 3 (10 pts): working 8-bit ripple-carry adder and 3-to-8 decoder tabs, built from primitive gates
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 3 (Combinational Logic). The first lab that intentionally does not finish in 90 minutes. Connects forward: this adder becomes the ALU core in Lab 6, and this decoder becomes RAM address decoding in Lab 8 and instruction decoding in Lab 11. Both are needed in Lab 5 and Lab 8, so finish them.

topics: Lab 4 — Latches, Flip-Flops, and Timing [Completes in class]
Build the NAND-based S-R latch from two cross-coupled NANDs; poke SET, remove SET, watch the output hold
Explore the forbidden state deliberately, then discuss why it must be engineered away
Build the gated D latch — add ENABLE, watch transparency
Build the edge-triggered D flip-flop, drive it from a Logisim clock, confirm it samples only on the rising edge
Timing diagram exercise: hand-draw D, CLK, and Q for the latch and the flip-flop given the same input sequence, then verify against poke-and-step behavior
Close: Quiz 1 concept sweep — a verbal walk back down the ladder from flip-flop to voltage
assignments: Completion check 4 (10 pts): S-R latch, gated D latch, and D flip-flop tabs, plus your hand-drawn timing diagrams
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 4 (Sequential Logic) and CSC 210's Quiz 1 week. The pivot point of the course — logic becomes memory. Labor Day is Monday 9/7; lab meets normally on Tuesday 9/8. Leaves lab with the memory primitives every remaining lab instances.

phases.title: Phase 2: Registers, ALU, and MIPS (Labs 5-8, Weeks 5-8)
phases.description: Split-format sessions — roughly 50 minutes Logisim, 40 minutes MARS. You work hardware and software on the same concept in the same session, which is the whole pedagogical point of this phase. Primary CSLOs: 1 and 2.

topics: Lab 5 — The 8-Bit Register & First MIPS Program [Finish on own]
Logisim (~50 min): instance eight of your own D flip-flops into a new tab; wire a shared clock
Add a LOAD control line so the register updates only when instructed; add tristate output enable so it can share a bus
Test protocol: load a value, change the inputs, confirm the stored value does not move
MARS (~40 min): tour the register file — $zero, $t0-$t9, $s0-$s7, $a0-$a3, $v0-$v1, $ra, $sp — and which you may clobber
Write and run a first program: load two immediates, add them, print with syscall
Single-step it and watch the Registers pane change one instruction at a time. Then the connection: the register you just built is what $t0 physically is
assignments: Completion check 5 (10 pts): working 8-bit register with LOAD and output enable, plus your first running MIPS program
Scaffolds CSC 210's Logisim Checkpoint 1 and MIPS Assignment 1 (graded in CSC 210, not here)
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 5. First split-format session — have both tools open before 2:00.

topics: Lab 6 — Building the ALU / MIPS Arithmetic [Finish on own]
Logisim (~50 min): start from your 8-bit adder and add subtraction by inverting operand B and forcing carry-in to 1 — two's complement stops being a formula and becomes a wire
Add AND, OR, and pass-through paths; use a decoder on the function-select lines to activate exactly one path
Add zero and negative flag outputs, needed for branches in Labs 11 and 14
Label and test unsigned overflow (255 + 1 → 0) and signed overflow (100 + 100 in two's complement) as two separate conditions with separate detection logic
MARS (~40 min): R-type drills add sub and or nor slt; I-type drills addi andi ori slti
Predict the register result before pressing step, every time
Closing connection: add $t0, $t1, $t2 routes two registers through the exact circuit on your screen
assignments: Completion check 6 (10 pts): working 8-bit ALU with decoder-based function select and both overflow flags, plus the arithmetic/logic MIPS drills
Scaffolds CSC 210's Logisim Checkpoint 2 and MIPS Assignment 2
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 6. Campus holiday is Friday 9/25; lab meets normally on Tuesday 9/22. Do not let unsigned and signed overflow blur together — they are different conditions with different detection logic.

topics: Lab 7 — Control Flow, Procedures, and the Stack [Finish on own] — MARS-dominant; the hardware track pauses to let assembly catch up
Branches: beq, bne, and building blt from slt + bne; watch the PC jump in the Text Segment pane
Loops: a counted loop and a sentinel loop, with breakpoints, stepped through
Jumps: j, jal, jr — and what jal actually does to $ra
The stack, visually: push and pop with $sp, watching the Data Segment pane grow downward in real time
Procedure calling convention: $a0-$a3 in, $v0-$v1 out, $ra for return, callee-saved vs. caller-saved
Recursion trace: step through a recursive factorial and watch stack frames stack up and unwind. Then the hardware hook — the ALU flags you built last week are what a branch instruction reads
assignments: Completion check 7 (10 pts): a procedure-writing exercise with a required recursive component, running in MARS
Scaffolds CSC 210's MIPS Assignment 3
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 7. Most students' first true understanding of the stack happens here rather than in lecture — watch the Data Segment pane, do not just read about it.

topics: Lab 8 — RAM Construction / MIPS Memory [Finish on own]
Logisim (~50 min): build a 4-to-16 decoder from gates, extending Lab 3's work
Instance sixteen 16-bit registers as rows and wire the decoder outputs to their LOAD lines — the 16x16 RAM matrix appears out of parts you already own
Add write-enable, a data bus, and a MAR to hold the address the CPU wants
Test: write to row 5, write something different to row 12, read both back
MARS (~40 min): lw, sw, lb, sb, and base + offset addressing
Declare an array in .data, walk it in a loop, watch the Data Segment pane light up; map int a[10] in C to 40 bytes to the addresses on screen
Closing connection: lw $t0, 0($s0) puts an address in the MAR, asserts read, and captures the output — the circuit you just built
assignments: Completion check 8 (10 pts): working RAM matrix with MAR, plus the array manipulation program
Scaffolds CSC 210's Logisim Checkpoint 3 and MIPS Assignment 4
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 8. CSC 210's midterm is this week, so the guided portion runs tight and the last 10 minutes are reserved for your questions. Come with them written down.

phases.title: Phase 3: CPU Design (Labs 9-12, Weeks 9-12)
phases.description: The parts become a machine. Integration, the register file, the control unit, and the bus — plus the file-hygiene audit that prevents the most common submission failure in this course. Primary CSLOs: 1 and 2.

topics: Lab 9 — Fetch-Decode-Execute & File Consolidation [Completes in class]
Trace exercise: whiteboard the fetch-decode-execute cycle for a single instruction, naming which component holds what at each step — PC, IR, MAR, MDR, ALU, register file
Run the same instruction in MARS single-step mode and correlate each pane on screen with each box on the whiteboard

File audit — the real point of this lab: open your .circ file and verify every circuit so far is a tab in that one file — S-R latch, D flip-flop, register, adder, decoder, ALU, RAM, MAR. Anyone building in separate files fixes it now, with help
Begin the top-level CPU tab: place components on a shared bus, no logic yet. Just the floor plan
assignments: Completion check 9 (10 pts): file audit passed — one .circ file, every circuit present as a tab, no external links — and the CPU floor-plan tab started
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 9 (Von Neumann Model). A deliberate integration and hygiene lab before the hard build weeks. The file-structure failure is the single most common submission problem in this course, and Week 9 is the last moment where fixing it is cheap.

topics: Lab 10 — Register File + ALU Integration [Finish on own]
Build the register file: R0-R3 plus PC and MAR, with decoder-based selection for read and write
Two read ports (the ALU needs two operands at once) and one write port
Wire the register file to the ALU: read A and read B into the ALU inputs, result back to the write port
Wire the flag outputs somewhere visible — they matter in Lab 11
Test protocol: load R1 and R2 by hand, select ADD, clock once, read R3
Last 20 minutes — Project Planning Workshop: draft your final project ISA on paper. Which instructions, what opcode encoding, what each does. The instructor circulates and reality-checks scope
assignments: Completion check 10 (10 pts): register file wired to the ALU and passing the test protocol, plus your drafted ISA on paper
Scaffolds CSC 210's Logisim Checkpoint 4 and the CPU project plan
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 10. Catching an over-ambitious ISA here saves you in Week 16 — bring your instruction ideas and let them get pushed back on now rather than later.

topics: Lab 11 — The Control Unit [Finish on own]
Add the IR to hold the current instruction

Build the control table on paper first: rows = opcodes, columns = control signals (RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, ALUSrc, ALUOp, Branch). Fill it in for a 3-4 instruction subset before touching Logisim — students who skip this step build spaghetti
Build the opcode decoder, then wire each output through OR gates to produce each control signal. The paper table translates to wiring almost mechanically
Test protocol: hand-load an opcode into the IR, clock, confirm exactly the expected control lines assert
Timing discussion with probes: why everything must settle before the next clock edge
assignments: Completion check 11 (10 pts): paper control table plus a working control unit for your instruction subset
Scaffolds CSC 210's Logisim Checkpoint 5
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 11. The lab where the machine gets a brain — and where you discover the brain is just a truth table. Extend the paper table to your full project ISA on your own time.

topics: Lab 12 — Bus, Memory Interface & Memory-Mapped I/O [Completes in class]
Logisim (~45 min): connect the CPU core to the RAM built in Lab 8 — address lines, data lines, control lines
Add the MDR as the buffer between CPU and memory
Trace a complete memory read and a complete memory write with probes, naming which signal asserts when
MARS (~35 min): syscall in depth — print integer, print string, read integer, exit
MARS Tools → Keyboard and Display MMIO Simulator: write to a memory address and a character appears on a simulated display. Memory-mapped I/O stops being an abstraction in about thirty seconds
Discussion: your Logisim RAM decoder could reserve an address that is not memory at all — that is all memory-mapped I/O is
Last 10 minutes: Quiz 2 concept sweep across Phase 3
assignments: Completion check 12 (10 pts): CPU-to-RAM interface with MDR, traced read and write, plus your MMIO demonstration
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 12 and CSC 210's Quiz 2 week. College deadline: 11/6/2026 is the last day to drop with a 'W' notation. Set by the college; the instructor cannot extend it. Talk to me and to Financial Aid before you drop.

phases.title: Phase 4: Integration and Modern Topics (Labs 13-17, Weeks 13-17)
phases.description: The datapath comes alive, then the build sequence closes and the remaining sessions cover modern architecture, verify submissions, and reserve time for catch-up. Lab 14 is the last circuit-build lab of the semester. Primary CSLOs: 1 and 2.

topics: Lab 13 — Datapath Integration: First Instructions Execute [Finish on own] — the payoff week
Wire the complete datapath: PC → instruction memory → IR → control unit → register file / ALU → write-back
Get MOV, ADD, and SUB executing end to end from an instruction stored in memory

Debugging clinic — the real skill of this lab. A systematic method rather than flailing: (1) does the PC advance? (2) does the IR hold the right bits? (3) do the control lines match your paper table? (4) do the register file's read ports show the right operands? (5) does the ALU output what you expect? (6) does write-back land in the right register?
Find the first step that fails — the bug is there, not downstream. The instructor demonstrates on a deliberately broken circuit
Celebrate out loud when the first instruction executes
assignments: Completion check 13 (10 pts): MOV, ADD, and SUB executing reliably from instructions stored in memory
Scaffolds CSC 210's Logisim Checkpoint 6
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 13. Veterans Day is Wednesday 11/11; lab meets normally on Tuesday 11/10. The debugging method taught here is the most transferable thing in the course — learn it deliberately, not accidentally.

topics: Lab 14 — Branches, Jumps, Memory Access, and Testing [Finish on own]
Implement branch: the ALU zero flag gates whether the PC loads a new value or increments. Everything needed was built in Labs 6, 10, and 11 — this is mostly wiring what already exists
Implement jump
Implement load and store against the RAM from Lab 8
Hand-assembly exercise: encode a short test program into your own machine code by hand and load it into instruction memory. Nothing teaches what an assembler does like being one for twenty minutes

Write your test program: one that exercises every implemented instruction, including a loop that terminates via branch. This is a CSC 210 final project deliverable — starting it here means it is not invented at 11 PM on 12/10
assignments: Completion check 14 (10 pts): 10 or more working instructions including branch, jump, and load/store, plus a passing test program
Scaffolds CSC 210's Logisim Checkpoint 7
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 14. This is the last lab that builds circuitry together. The remaining sessions cover performance and modern architecture and reserve time for CPU catch-up, but from here forward progress on the simulation itself is self-directed. A student who leaves Lab 14 without branch, jump, and load/store working is relying on independent work from that point on — so push hard this week, and use the reserved time in Labs 15 and 16 if you fall behind.

topics: Lab 15 — Performance Measurement [Completes in class] — a required session, deliberately light, with no new Logisim work

Performance measurement (~55 min). MARS Tools → Instruction Counter / Instruction Statistics: run two programs that compute the same result — one naive, one optimized — and compare instruction counts. Measured, not asserted
Apply the performance equation, Time = Instructions × CPI × Clock Period, to your own measured counts
Amdahl's Law worksheet: speed up the 20% of your program that dominates nothing by 10x and compute what actually happens. Do the arithmetic yourself — the result usually surprises people
Pipelining introduced as a paper exercise: the laundry / assembly-line analogy drawn as a timing chart, setting up Lab 16's hazard trace

Reserved catch-up time (~30 min): open one-on-one debugging on Labs 13 and 14. If your datapath is not executing, or branch/jump/memory are not working, this time is for you. If you are caught up, finish the worksheet and leave early
assignments: Completion check 15 (10 pts): completed performance worksheet with your own measured instruction counts and Amdahl's Law calculations
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 15. Thanksgiving holiday is 11/25-11/29; lab meets normally on Tuesday 11/24. This session is entirely self-contained, requires no prior circuit, and nothing later depends on it — the worksheet and MARS tool steps are published in writing, so if you travel early you can complete it on your own without falling behind.

topics: Lab 16 — Cache Behavior, Pipeline Hazards & Peer Testing [Completes in class]

Modern architecture (~50 min). MARS Tools → Data Cache Simulator: traverse a 2-D array row-major and record the hit rate, change one line to traverse it column-major and record it again. Same work, dramatically different performance — locality of reference becomes a number you produced yourself
Vary cache size, block size, and associativity in the tool, re-run, and chart the results
Pipeline hazard hand-trace: given a short MIPS sequence with a data dependency, draw the 5-stage pipeline diagram and identify where a stall or a forward is required
Place cache in the memory hierarchy against the RAM circuit built in Lab 8 — same address decoding idea, different speed tier

Peer testing & submission verification (~35 min). Circuit swap: exchange .circ files and run each other's test programs on the partner's CPU. Fresh eyes find missing instructions, unhandled cases, and — critically — broken external file links, while there is still a week to fix them

Submission checklist, verified live on your own file: all circuits contained in this single .circ file with no external links; the file opens and functions on a machine that has never seen your other files; 10+ instructions implemented and tested; at least one branch or jump works; at least one load or store works; the test program exercises every implemented instruction; written documentation covers design decisions, ISA definition, and test results
assignments: Completion check 16 (10 pts): cache experiment results, pipeline hazard trace, and a completed peer-test report on a partner's CPU
weeks.notes: Supports Lecture Step 16 (Modern Architecture). Last structured session and the last time the whole room is together before the CSC 210 final project is due, so the submission checks happen here. Anyone flagged at risk during this session should plan to come to Lab 17.

topics: Lab 17 — Free Work Period & Open Q&A [Unstructured] — no agenda: the room, the instructor, and three days before the deadline
Open Q&A on the 8-bit CPU simulation — any question, any component, any bug. Students who have been quiet all semester tend to ask here; the space is left for it
Work time on the final project, with the instructor circulating for one-on-one debugging
Documentation help — the written component (design decisions, ISA definition, test results) is where otherwise-strong projects lose points. If you have a working circuit and no write-up, come here

grading._basis: Completion checks on lab work, chosen by the instructor 2026-08-17 (Open Item #1 of the topical outline). Sixteen checks at 10 points each = 160 points. Lab 17 carries no check, so nothing in this course penalizes skipping the free work period. The grade is entirely independent of CSC 210: no CSC 210 grade depends on lab attendance or on any lab completion check, and no lab check requires a CSC 210 submission.

breakdown.description: Four checks at 10 points: toolchain and semester .circ file created (Lab 1); NAND-built gate library and De Morgan verifier (Lab 2); 8-bit adder and 3-to-8 decoder (Lab 3); S-R latch, gated D latch, D flip-flop, and timing diagrams (Lab 4).

Four checks at 10 points: 8-bit register plus first MIPS program (Lab 5); ALU with decoder select and both overflow flags, plus arithmetic drills (Lab 6); recursive procedure exercise in MARS (Lab 7); RAM matrix with MAR plus array program (Lab 8).

Four checks at 10 points: single-file audit passed and CPU floor plan started (Lab 9); register file wired to the ALU plus your drafted ISA (Lab 10); paper control table plus working control unit (Lab 11); CPU-to-RAM interface with MDR plus the MMIO demonstration (Lab 12).

Four checks at 10 points: MOV/ADD/SUB executing (Lab 13); 10+ instructions with branch, jump, and load/store plus a test program (Lab 14); performance worksheet with your own measured counts (Lab 15); cache experiment, hazard trace, and peer-test report (Lab 16). Lab 17 has no check — the free work period is never graded.

required: Logisim Classic 2.7.1 - used for every circuit you build. Not Logisim Evolution; the two behave differently and this lab is built around Classic. Free download for Windows and macOS from the course SharePoint. Installed and verified in Lab 1.
MARS (MIPS Assembler and Runtime Simulator) - used for all assembly-language work. Free, Java-based. Installed and verified in Lab 1.

Your semester .circ file - you create LastName_CSC210.circ in Lab 1 and every circuit for the rest of the term becomes a new tab in that same file, never a separate file with external links. We do a 30-second file check at the start of every session.
The CSC 210 AI Tutor - the one approved AI tool for this course, web-based, introduced in Week 2. Free, no account beyond your college login. See the AI Policy under Policies & Resources.

A laptop you can run Logisim and MARS on during the Zoom session, plus a reliable enough connection to share your screen when you need help debugging. Both tools are Java-based and run on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
optional: Primary reference (free): Saylor Academy, CS301: Computer Architecture - free, openly licensed, self-paced. Shared with CSC 210. CS301 syllabus and units

Recommended: Plantz, R. G., Introduction to Computer Organization: An Under the Hood Look at Hardware and x86-64 Assembly (No Starch Press). Pairs especially well with the 8-bit circuit builds in Labs 5-8.

Reference only, not assigned: Patterson, D. A., & Hennessy, J. L., Computer Organization and Design, MIPS Edition (Morgan Kaufmann). A second reference for the MIPS instruction set and the performance and pipelining material in Labs 15-16.

Graph paper or a notebook. Labs 4, 11, 14, and 16 all involve drawing before building - timing diagrams, control tables, hand-assembly, and pipeline traces. Paper first is not optional advice; it is how these labs are designed.

workload.breakdown: 1.5 hrs synchronous Tuesday Zoom lab + approximately 1.5 hrs asynchronous work between sessions (finishing [Finish on own] builds, drills, and worksheets)
workload.notes: Ninety minutes of instruction every Tuesday across 17 weeks is about 25.5 synchronous contact hours, with a comparable asynchronous portion between sessions. The asynchronous load is not evenly distributed by design: labs marked [Completes in class] (Labs 1, 2, 4, 9, 12, 15, 16) leave you with little or nothing to finish, while labs marked [Finish on own] (Labs 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14) deliberately send you home with a working partial circuit and a short remaining task, typically 45-90 minutes. Labs 13 and 14 run heaviest; Lab 15 is deliberately light and Lab 17 is unstructured. Circuit debugging is unpredictable by nature - start the remaining task early in the week rather than on Monday night.

policies.attendance: This lab meets live on Zoom every Tuesday from 2:00 to 3:20 PM, and the sessions are the point of the course - the guided build, the instructor at the front stopping at checkpoints, and the circulating help while you debug. Come. That said, your grade is based on the weekly completion checks, not on attendance, and every check is completable by a student who missed the session: the build steps and any worksheets are published in writing each week. If you have to miss a Tuesday, work through that week's material and submit the check on time; if you are missing several in a row, email me early rather than late. This course builds continuously - Lab 10's circuit instances Lab 4's flip-flop - so a missed week is not a week you can skip past. Lab 17 is ungraded and carries no attendance expectation at all.
policies.lateWork: Completion checks have a standing 48-hour grace window with no penalty and no need to ask; after that, contact me and we will work something out. Because each build feeds the next, a late check costs you more in momentum than in points - the grace window exists so that a hard week does not compound. This course-specific policy replaces the general late-submission statement shown under Policies & Resources.
policies.makeupExams: There are no exams, quizzes, or a final exam in CSC 210L. The entire grade is the sixteen weekly completion checks. If an emergency costs you a week, submit the check late under the grace window or contact me - there is nothing here that has to be made up under exam conditions.
policies.academicIntegrity:
See the AI Policy for This Course under Policies & Resources for the governing statement on AI in CSC 210L. It is identical to the CSC 210 policy: the course AI Tutor is the one approved AI tool and you may use it as much as you like; general-purpose AI assistants are not permitted on graded work.

Beyond AI, ordinary academic honesty applies, with one lab-specific note: collaboration in this room is encouraged and expected. The whole point of the guided build is that we do it together, and Lab 16 has you deliberately test a partner's CPU. Working alongside someone, comparing approaches, and finding each other's bugs is exactly right. What is not right is submitting a circuit or a program you did not build - a partner's file, a downloaded file, or a generated one. You should be able to explain any part of what you submit on request. Academic dishonesty falls under the College Academic Honesty Policy (AP 5500.2) and may result in a failing grade on the assignment or in the course, plus referral for disciplinary action. If you are unsure whether something crosses a line, ask me before you submit.
policies._labIndependence: Not rendered. Standing design constraint from the topical outline: lab is a recommended, not required, companion course. No CSC 210 grade may depend on lab attendance or on any CSC 210L completion check, and every Logisim Checkpoint, MIPS assignment, and the Final Project must remain fully completable by a student who never sets foot in lab. Lab reduces friction; it does not gate the grade.
